doc.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Peace Piece and spontaneous creation in the studio
summary: Rowe plays Peace Piece, and Keepnews explains it was improvised as an intro to Some Other Time and spliced from two takes.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Speaking of him I wanted to get your reaction on this if I could. Let’s see if I found the kind of, this is like a blindfold test.
Since I don’t know what you put on. Okay.
I always wondered what was going on in the booth especially.

Well “Peace Piece” is literally what it always was identified as being. “Peace Piece” was an improvisation, it is true that what he was setting out to do was to create an introduction to a recording of “Some Other Time,” the Leonard Bernstein, Comden and Green song. He started messing around and found that gee, this was something very interesting in and of itself so that literally that was created at the record date. I mean nobody went in there with the intention — now actually the title was in existence but not to be used on that tune. There is a solo piece called “Epilogue” which is on the end of each side of that album originally. That was originally going to be called “Peace Piece.” So the title was there and then this thing was created, and this goes much better with that title, but it literally was a spontaneously generated thing. And the interesting part of that is, a couple of interesting stories. One is although unfortunately the tape for some reason did not survive as sometimes happens, nobody thought in terms of alternates and whatnot, “Peace Piece” as issued is approximately fifty percent from one take and fifty percent from another. If you like the beginning of — I think he just did it twice. He liked the beginning of one, liked the end of the other, obviously no problem splicing together. But it sure would have been nice at some stage of the game to be able to issue the rejected halves, but they did not survive for whatever reason. And that frequently happens. Oh yeah, session takes that the good things have been taken out of, where are they? It doesn’t matter. So that is one point. Also he maintained for years that he couldn’t play it again because it had never been notated and it just existed as free improvisation. Towards the end though I do believe he had gotten himself to where he played it, he re-created it and played it a few times. But essentially it was what it was, a total improvisation starting from an initial concept which was that he was trying to do something that would fit as an intro to “Some Other Time.”
Right. Did you have a feeling when it was over that this is going on the album, right away?

Well actually what happens is when anything gets done at a record session the only unusual thought I’m going to have is gee this is lousy, this is not going to go on the album. We’re in the studio to make the album, why not start with that. And even something that’s added like that, because after all jazz is a music of improvisation is it not? So it’s not a matter of gee, isn’t that wonderful. It’s probably gee isn’t it wonderful we didn’t waste our damn time, studio time is expensive.
